videos.title: Russia Gets New Year 11 Times?! 🇷🇺🎆 #russia #timetravel #christmas
videos.description:
Why does Russia have 11 time zones, and which country has the most time zones in the world? Russia's time zones explained in 40 seconds.

When Kamchatka hits midnight on New Year's Eve, Kaliningrad is still at 2 PM. In 2010 Russia cut its time zones from 11 to 9, people in Kamchatka protested, and by 2014 both zones were back. Until 2018, long-distance train timetables ran on Moscow time, so a 7 PM ticket could mean 2 AM in Vladivostok. And the world record? France has 12 time zones, thanks to its islands all over the planet.

videos.title: World's Longest Flight Ever?! ✈️ #france #australia #flight
videos.description:
The world's longest flight by a commercial airliner: an Airbus A350-1000ULR flew non-stop from Melbourne, Australia to Toulouse, France in 24 hours 24 minutes, 23,155 km.
And it went the "wrong" way: east over the Pacific, America and the Atlantic, not west past India.

The short way from Melbourne to France is about 17,000 km. On 27-28 July 2026, the Qantas Project Sunrise test jet flew east instead, saw two sunsets and two sunrises, and landed in Toulouse. Guinness confirmed the record in November 2026. Because a distance record counts distance, not direction. The record it broke: a Boeing 777-200LR, Hong Kong to London on 9-10 November 2005, 21,601 km, also flown the long way east. Controllers even offered it shortcuts. The pilots said no.

videos.title: Single Lake Holds More Water Than 5 Great Lakes 🤯
videos.description:
Lake Baikal vs the Great Lakes: how the deepest lake in the world holds more water than all five combined.
Baikal in Siberia is barely bigger than Belgium, yet it plunges 1,642 metres.

It fills a crack in the Earth that opened about 25–30 million years ago, which makes it the oldest lake known. The crack is still widening by about 4 mm a year. Below the lake floor lie up to 7 km of mud, and the rift goes down roughly as far as Everest is tall.

videos.title: This River runs across 4 Countries?! 🤯
videos.description:
Why does the Danube flow through 4 capital cities, and where does part of it disappear? The Danube Sinkhole at Immendingen, Germany, on a 3D map.

The Danube runs through Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade, more capitals than any other river, and touches 10 countries on its way to the Black Sea. Vienna and Bratislava are only about 56 km apart. But near its source at Immendingen, the riverbed is cracked limestone and the water drains into the ground; in 1921 that stretch was completely dry on 309 days. An 1877 salt and dye test found the water about 60 hours later at the Aach spring, roughly 12 km south, which flows into Lake Constance and the Rhine, and on to the North Sea. Geologists think the upper Danube may one day drain to the Rhine for good.

videos.title: Spain Has 5 Neighbours?! 🇪🇸🤯
videos.description:
Spain's neighbouring countries aren't just Portugal and France: Spain borders 5 countries, including Morocco in Africa, plus a Spanish town inside France and an island that changes country every 6 months.

Spain's land neighbours are Portugal, France, Andorra, the UK (through Gibraltar) and Morocco (around Ceuta, Melilla and the Peñón de Vélez de la Gomera). In 1934 a storm built a sand bar that joined the Peñón to the African coast, creating a border of about 85 metres. In 1659 Spain and France signed the Treaty of the Pyrenees on Pheasant Island; the follow-up deal handed France 33 villages, but Llívia was a town, so it stayed Spanish and is now surrounded by France. Pheasant Island itself is shared: Spanish from 1 February to 31 July and French from 1 August to 31 January, an arrangement in force since 1902. Nobody lives there.

videos.title: Is Russia Bigger Than Pluto? 🇷🇺🤔
videos.description:
Is Russia bigger than Pluto? Russia covers about 17.1 million km², and for decades Pluto's whole surface was thought to be smaller. Then NASA's New Horizons flew past Pluto in 2015 and measured it.

Through Hubble, Pluto looked about 2,300 km wide, which gives a surface of about 16.6 million km², so Russia won. In 2006 Pluto was voted out of the planet club. Then, after a 9.5-year trip, New Horizons measured Pluto at 2,377 km wide: a surface of about 17.7 million km². Pluto beats Russia by about 650,000 km², almost a whole Texas. And half of Pluto's famous heart, Sputnik Planitia, is named after Sputnik 1, the Soviet Union's first satellite.

videos.title: 6 Turkey Facts That Sound Fake 🇹🇷🤯
videos.description:
6 facts about Turkey (Türkiye) that sound fake: Istanbul on two continents, a whole sea inside one country, Santa Claus's real hometown, the Derinkuyu underground city and Göbekli Tepe.
Plus the twist: why a bird shares the country's name, and what Turks and Hindi speakers call it. COP31 is being held in Antalya, Turkey, from 9 to 20 November 2026.

About 97% of Turkey is in Asia, yet its biggest city, Istanbul, straddles the Bosphorus, and the capital is Ankara. The Sea of Marmara lies entirely inside Turkey and is often called the world's smallest sea. Saint Nicholas, who inspired Santa Claus, was bishop of Myra, today's Demre in Antalya province. The story goes that in 1963 a man renovating his house in Derinkuyu broke through a wall and found an underground city about 85 m deep, built for up to 20,000 people and their animals. Göbekli Tepe's stone pillars were raised about 11,500 years ago, roughly 6,000 years before Stonehenge. The bird is called "turkey" in English after guineafowl traded through Ottoman lands; Turks call it "hindi" and Hindi calls it "peru". Since 2022 the UN uses "Türkiye".

videos.title: Why SPACEX launches Rockets From Here? 🚀
videos.description:
Why does SpaceX launch Starship from Starbase, a lonely beach at the tip of Texas just a few km from Mexico? The answer is Earth's spin, the open Gulf to the east, and a plan to catch the ship with the tower's giant 'chopsticks'.

Earth turns east, and at Starbase's latitude (about 26°N) the ground moves at roughly 1,500 km/h, so a rocket launched east gets that speed for free. East of the pad lies over a thousand kilometres of open sea, so anything that goes wrong falls in the water, not on a city. Starbase also sits a little closer to the equator than Florida's Cape Canaveral. SpaceX has caught the Super Heavy booster before, but never the ship: on Flight 15 (targeted for 13 Nov 2026) the plan is for the ship to loop Earth about 14 times, re-enter over the Pacific, fly over northern Mexico and the Rio Grande Valley, cross the Gulf and turn back to the tower called Mechazilla. Plans and dates can change.

videos.title: NASA Found a Skull in Antarctica 💀
videos.description:
NASA's new satellite photo shows a skull on Vega Island, Antarctica, staring straight at Devil Island. Here's what made it, plus 4 more Antarctica facts that sound fake.

The "skull" is made of landforms: a rock peak (a nunatak) for the eye, a glacier moraine for the grin and Devil's Bay Glacier for the jaw. It stands out because a warm 2026 winter left little snow to cover the ice. Antarctica also holds Earth's coldest recorded temperature (−89.2 °C at Vostok Station, 1983), a liquid lake under about 4 km of ice, and ground about 3.5 km below sea level under the Denman Glacier. And on Vega Island itself, scientists found the skull of Vegavis, a bird about 69 million years old and an early relative of ducks.

videos.title: 6 Australia Facts That Can't Be Real 🇦🇺🤯
videos.description:
6 Australia facts that sound fake but are true: Australia is wider than the Moon, drifts 7 cm a year, imported camels, built the 5,614 km Dingo Fence and lost the Great Emu War of 1932.
Australia facts, the Emu War explained, and why the whole country moved 1.8 metres on the map.

Australia is almost 4,000 km wide; the Moon is about 3,474 km across. The continent drifts about 7 cm a year, so in 2017 its official coordinates moved 1.8 m. At least 15,000 camels arrived between 1870 and 1900, most from British India; when trucks took over they were set free, and today Australia has the world's biggest wild camel herd. The Dingo Fence runs 5,614 km. And in November 1932, about 20,000 emus raided Western Australian wheat farms: two machine guns and 10,000 rounds later, the soldiers went home.

videos.title: It Hasn't Rained Here in 2 Million Years?!
videos.description:
The McMurdo Dry Valleys in Antarctica: why one of the driest places on Earth has almost no ice, and why NASA has tested Mars ideas here since the Viking missions.

The story goes, it hasn't rained here in about two million years. What's measured: mountains hold back the ice sheet, katabatic winds with gusts near 140 km/h scour the valleys, and the little snow that falls (around 10 cm a year) can turn straight to vapour within hours. Nothing rots: seals that wandered inland lie freeze-dried, some perhaps 2,000 years old. And microbes still live just under the surface of the rocks.

The 5 biggest countries in the world by area: Russia, Canada, the USA, China and Brazil.

Russia is about 17.1 million km² across 11 time zones. Canada is just under 10 million km² and has the longest coastline on Earth (about 243,000 km). Add lakes and coastal waters and the US moves ahead (about 9.8 vs 9.6). The gap is under 3%.

videos.title: Black Friday's Dark Secret! Police Hated Black Friday?! 🚓
videos.description:
Black Friday was named by the police, not by shops. In the 1950s, Philadelphia police used it for the chaotic day after Thanksgiving: traffic jams, crowds and shoplifters. Retailers hated it and in 1961 tried to rebrand it "Big Friday". Nobody listened. The original "Black Friday" was 24 September 1869, when two Wall Street speculators tried to corner the gold market and crashed it.

The name only spread nationally in the 1980s, and now Black Friday runs in well over a hundred countries that don't celebrate Thanksgiving, from the UK and Brazil to India, where it lands next to Diwali sales. Meanwhile China's Singles Day is bigger still: Alibaba alone sold about $38 billion in one day in 2019, more than US Black Friday and Cyber Monday online sales combined. This year, Black Friday is on 27 November.

videos.title: Britain Burns a Man Every Year?! 🤯
videos.description:
Every 5 November, Britain lights bonfires and burns a "guy" on top. The reason: in 1605, thirteen plotters hid 36 barrels of gunpowder under the House of Lords to blow up King James I. An anonymous letter gave them away, and on the night of 4 November guards found Guy Fawkes in the cellar with the matches.

Parliament made 5 November a compulsory day of thanksgiving by law (the Observance of 5th November Act 1606), which stayed in force for about 250 years until 1859. Fawkes himself was never burned: he jumped from the gallows and broke his neck. Today, Lewes in Sussex, a town of about 17,000, draws up to 80,000 people and carries 17 burning crosses, and the Yeomen of the Guard still search Parliament's cellars before every State Opening.

videos.description:
In Monaco, citizens aren't allowed into the gaming rooms of the famous Monte Carlo Casino. Monaco is only about 2 km², smaller than New York's Central Park, and about 39,000 people live there, but fewer than 1 in 4 are actual Monégasque citizens. Many moved in because there's no personal income tax.

The casino was built in the 1860s to save the principality's finances with visitors' money, not locals'. Monaco is also running out of room, so it builds land into the sea: its newest district, opened in 2024, added about 6 hectares worth around €1 billion. And its whole coastline is under 4 km.

videos.title: Canada Is South of Rome?! 🇨🇦
videos.description:
Canada's southernmost point, Middle Island in Lake Erie, sits at about 41.68° N. Rome is at about 41.9° N, so Canada's tip is further south than Rome, and even south of California's northern border (42° N). Toronto (about 43.65° N) is further south than Monaco (43.73° N), and in Windsor, Ontario, you drive north to reach Detroit in the USA.

So why does Canada feel so far north? Because Europe is further north than most people think: Paris is north of Montreal, London is north of Calgary. Europe stays milder thanks to the Gulf Stream, a warm ocean current from the Gulf of Mexico, while Canada gets the Arctic air.

videos.title: 5 Countries Fought Over a Lake?! 🌊
videos.description:
The world's biggest lake is called a sea. The Caspian covers about 370,000 km², bigger than Germany, and holds roughly 40% of all the lake water on Earth. It's salty, but only about a third as salty as the ocean, and its surface sits about 28 metres below sea level.

Five countries share it: Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan. With oil and gas underneath, "sea or lake?" was worth billions: a sea is divided under maritime law, a lake between its shores. After more than 20 years of talks, the five signed a convention in 2018 that gave it a special status, neither fully a sea nor a lake. Meanwhile it's shrinking: in 2025 its level hit the lowest ever recorded.

videos.title: The Diwali Photo That Fooled India 🛰️
videos.description:
Every Diwali, a colourful "India from space on Diwali night" picture goes viral. It's not that. It's real satellite data, but not from Diwali and not from one night: a NOAA scientist made it in 2003 to show how India's city lights grew. Each colour is a year: white lights existed before 1992, blue appeared in 1992, green in 1998 and red in 2003.

What does real Diwali look like from space? NASA checked in 2012: the extra light was so subtle it's likely invisible from orbit. This year Diwali is on 8 November. When this photo shows up again, you'll know.

videos.title: Countries That Got Cheated on Coastline 🌊
videos.description:
Croatia's Pelješac Bridge project cost about €420 million (mostly EU-funded), just to avoid driving through 20 km of Bosnia. Some countries got the sea's leftovers: DR Congo, Africa's second-biggest country, has just 37 km of coastline. Iraq has over 430,000 km² of land and 58 km of coast. Jordan has 26 km on the Red Sea at Aqaba.

Bosnia and Herzegovina has about 20 km of coast and one seaside town, Neum, and that strip cuts Croatia in two. So Croatia built a 2.4 km bridge to go around it, opened in 2022. And the smallest coast of all? Monaco, about 4 km.

videos.title: Why France Borders Brazil 🤯
videos.description:
France's longest land border isn't with Spain. It's with Brazil. French Guiana, on the north coast of South America, isn't a colony: it's a full region of France and part of the European Union, so it uses the euro and EU rules on the edge of the Amazon. Its border with Brazil runs along the Oyapock River for about 650 to 730 km, depending on who measures, longer than the France–Spain border (about 623 km).

Europe launches its rockets from Kourou, about 500 km north of the equator, where Earth's spin gives rockets a free push. And the only bridge across the border was finished in 2011, but didn't open until March 2017. Six years, and nobody crossed.

videos.title: 40% of Canada is Almost Empty?! 🇨🇦
videos.description:
Canada has 10 provinces and 3 territories: Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut. Together the territories cover about 39% of Canada, more than all of India, yet only about 136,000 people live there, roughly 0.3% of Canadians, about one Narendra Modi Stadium.

Nunavut alone is about 2 million km², almost as big as Mexico, and its capital Iqaluit has no road to any other town. Provinces get their powers from Canada's constitution; territories get theirs from Ottawa through federal laws. The Northwest Territories and Nunavut have no political parties in their legislatures and govern by consensus, and in 2027 Nunavut takes control of its own land and resources.

videos.title: An Iceberg the Size of London?! 🧊
videos.description:
Iceberg A-81 broke off Antarctica's Brunt Ice Shelf, near the UK's Halley research station, in January 2023. At roughly 1,300–1,500 km², it is about the size of Greater London.

Over three years it drifted about 2,300 km through the Weddell Sea, past the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula and into the Scotia Sea, and in October 2026 it stalled off South Georgia. Ocean currents carry most Antarctic icebergs north through "iceberg alley" toward this island. A grounded giant can block penguins and seals from their feeding grounds (about half the world's southern elephant seals breed here), but as it melts it also releases nutrients that feed the ocean. videos.title: WHY DO STARS TWINKLE?!
videos.description:
Why do stars twinkle, and why don't planets? The twinkle isn't the star at all: it's about 100 km of moving air above your head.

Starlight from Sirius travels about 8.6 years to reach you, then gets bent around by warm and cold pockets of air in roughly its last third of a millisecond. Stars are so far away that their light arrives as a single point, so every pocket of air shoves it brighter, dimmer, left and right. Planets are much closer and show a tiny disc, so they usually shine steady. That's why astronomers climb: Chile's Atacama Desert hosts telescopes over 2,600 m up, India's Hanle observatory in Ladakh sits at about 4,500 m inside India's first dark sky reserve, Europe's new 39 m telescope will reshape a mirror about 1,000 times a second, and Hubble simply orbits about 480 km up, above the air.

videos.title: Halley's Comet Is 5 Billion km Away. So Why Is It Here?
videos.description:
Halley's Comet is hitting your sky right now: the Orionid meteor shower is Halley's dust. Here's how a comet over 5 billion km away still reaches Earth.

Every 76 years or so, Halley swings past the Sun and sheds dust that stays spread along its orbit. Earth crosses that trail twice a year: in May (the Eta Aquariids) and in October (the Orionids). Halley orbits the "wrong way", so we hit its dust head-on at about 66 km per second, roughly Delhi to Mumbai in 17 seconds. Each sand-sized grain burns up around 100 km above you, best seen after midnight from both hemispheres. Halley itself is due back in July 2061.

Homo sapiens in Africa, Neanderthals in Europe, Denisovans in Siberia and East Asia, the last Homo erectus on Java, the one-metre "Hobbits" of Flores (Homo floresiensis) and Homo luzonensis in the Philippines, only named in 2019. By about 40,000 years ago the Neanderthals were gone, and one by one the others vanished. But our ancestors had children with them: people with roots in Europe or Asia carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA, and in Papua New Guinea it's up to about 5% Denisovan.

videos.title: Why Bengaluru Has 1,000s of Lakes but No River 🇮🇳
videos.description:
Why does Bengaluru have so many lakes when it has no big river? The history of Bengaluru's lakes, from 9th-century tanks to the Majestic bus stand.

Bengaluru sits on a ridge about 920 m up, with no major river nearby. So for more than 1,100 years, people built earth embankments across the valleys to trap monsoon rain, creating chains of tanks that overflow from one into the next: six cascading chains across three valleys. Kempegowda, who founded the city in 1537, kept building more. Then the city grew over them: from 1973 to 2013, about 79% of its water bodies vanished, and today water is pumped about 100 km from the Kaveri and lifted about 300 m. Some lost lakes are hiding in plain sight: Kanteerava Stadium (Sampangi Lake), KR Market (Siddikatte) and Majestic bus stand (Dharmambudhi).

But today's lines are drawn by governments: China runs one time zone across the whole country, France has 12, Samoa deleted a Friday in 2011, and Nepal sits 15 minutes ahead of India.
